ch08 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
chapters.relation: Sanders reads Casino as a dramatization of ethical egoism, using the parasitic bond between Nicky Santoro and Ace Rothstein to ask whether an egoist who treats a friend as a mere instrument can have real friendship. He distinguishes 'maximizing' egoism (Nicky's ruinous take-everything drive, ending in his beating death) from a 'satisficing' egoism that restricts its own dispositions, arguing against Blum, Wilcox and an Aristotelian objection that only the maximizing version is truly incompatible with friendship. Aristotle's account of virtue and friendship supplies the standard the film's egoists fall short of.

chapters.file: ch09 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
chapters.relation: Skoble uses Taxi Driver's Travis Bickle to probe when vigilantism is justified, invoking Locke's claim that in civil society individuals delegate private vengeance to the state for objectivity. He argues Travis's rescue of the trapped child prostitute Iris is legitimate (the police won't help, she can't help herself) while his plan to assassinate Senator Palantine is madness, drawing the key line between correctly identifying a deserving target and mere perceived evil (contrasting Travis with Death Wish's Kersey, Batman, and Klan lynch mobs). He closes with Socrates' 'unexamined life' as the remedy: contemplating justice so we can confront real badness rather than turn away.

chapters.file: ch10 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
chapters.relation: Kowalski likens Goodfellas' Henry Hill to Plato's Gyges: both act immorally with near-total impunity, posing Glaucon's challenge in the Republic of why one should be just when one can escape all consequences. He applies Plato's tripartite soul (appetitive, spirited, rational) to Henry (runaway appetite/cocaine), Tommy (overstretched spirit, killing Billy Batts and Spider out of wounded pride) and cool, untroubled Paulie, treating them as the disharmonious 'unbalanced self.' Against the objection that these gangsters seem happy, he deploys Plato's health/happiness analogy and the feeling-happy vs being-happy distinction to argue they suffer 'cancer of the soul' and cannot be truly happy.

chapters.file: ch11 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
chapters.relation: Conard uses Mean Streets' guilt-ridden Charlie to survey conceptions of unhappiness against three definitions of happiness: beatitude (Aquinas), pleasure (Mill's hedonism), and flourishing (Aristotle's eudaimonia). He reads Charlie as damned in his own Catholic eyes, then invokes Nietzsche's Genealogy that religion manufactures guilt from internalized instinct, Plato's disordered soul and akrasia to explain Charlie's conflicting desires, and Schopenhauer's and Freud's pessimism that suffering is our natural state. He argues Charlie reaches dysdaimonia by acquiring vices and pursuing an ignoble (gangster) life, closing with Plato's Symposium and Sartre's facticity/transcendence to cast unhappiness as an ontological lack at the heart of human desire.

chapters.file: ch12 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
ch13 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
chapters.relation: Abrams argues Scorsese's key protagonists embody a Nietzschean 'cinema of madness' distinct from the merely destructive gangster: creative madmen who, like Nietzsche's Gay Science madman and Zarathustra, destroy old values and will new ones. He reads Cape Fear's Nietzsche-reading Cady, Taxi Driver's Travis (whose 'true force' is a will to power revaluing society), Last Temptation's Jesus (a mad revaluator of the law, glossed via Foucault's Madness and Civilization), the failed witness Frank Pierce in Bringing Out the Dead, and The Aviator's Howard Hughes as figures channeling divine madness. He ties them to Plato's Phaedrus/Ion and Nietzsche's death of God and overman, insisting the true madman stands outside the herd to remake reality.

chapters.file: ch14 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
chapters.relation: Knight opens by denying that fiction films (Scorsese's included) actually 'do' philosophy, arguing they raise philosophical themes rather than construct arguments or thought experiments, then reads The Age of Innocence for its themes. Her thesis is that Scorsese renders the 'social semiotics' of 1870s New York high society—flowers, cutlery, seating, hand-kissing, the yellow-versus-red roses—as a code that constrains individual desire, with the outsider Countess Olenska as the catalyst who exposes its rigidity. Newland Archer is trapped between belonging and fleeing, and society (via May and the van der Luydens) quietly conspires to ship Ellen back to Europe and preserve the status quo, the camera and omniscient narrator judging the judges.

chapters.file: ch15 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
chapters.relation: McMahon argues After Hours uses dark comedy to reveal the existential truth that anyone, at any moment, is vulnerable to absurdity. She sets Sartre's account (absurdity as the contingency of existence, fled via bad faith) beside Camus' (absurdity as a feeling born of the clash between human need for order and the world's silence), then maps Paul Hackett's nightmarish SoHo night onto Sartre's Nausea (the ordinary Roquentin overwhelmed by objects and people) and No Exit ('hell is other people'), where others become the mechanism that discloses the absurd. She contends comedy, like horror, exploits our fascination with grim spectacle, and that laughing at absurdity—rather than horrific spectacle—lets audiences acknowledge and manage existential anxiety and still live well.
